1317.title: Inward path close
1317.hook: the stations, the diseases, the manners, the virtues: one heart, rusted and polished
1317.howItsDone: Muslims who follow the inward path work on the heart through repentance, remembrance and good manners, treating the stations, the diseases of the heart and the virtues as one discipline of purifying it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ihsan, excellence in everything, the way every virtue gets done. Today the inward path closes, and the whole road comes into view at once.

A copper pot left in a damp shed goes dull, then green. Nobody did anything to it. It just sat, and the air did the rest. Bring it inside, rub it with a cloth, and the shine comes back, a patch at a time. The Qur'an uses that picture for the heart. In surah al-Mutaffifin, in Pickthall's translation: "Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts." Rust can gather. And what gathers can be wiped.
screen: `A COPPER POT GOES DULL.` → `RUST UPON THEIR HEARTS.` → `WHAT GATHERS CAN BE WIPED.`

segments.voice: Start where the heart days started: the lump of flesh. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: in the body is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Truly, it is the heart. Then Jami' at-Tirmidhi explains the rust. In paraphrase: when a servant sins, a black spot is marked on his heart. If he leaves it, seeks forgiveness and repents, his heart is polished. If he returns to it, the spot spreads, and that, the hadith says, is the rust Allah mentions. Now the whole road, through that picture. The stations, among them repentance, watchfulness, patience, gratitude, reliance, love, sincerity: the way the heart is meant to face. The diseases: arrogance, envy, showing off, anger, greed, backbiting, lying, heedlessness, despair: the rust itself, named one by one so it can be seen. The manners, the adab: of speech, eating, guests, travel, sleep, learning, the road and the market, with parents, neighbors, children, animals and the earth: the daily cloth, small wipes. The virtues: humility, generosity, modesty, truthfulness, pardon, gentleness, justice, ties of kin, loving for others, contentment, and ihsan over all of them: the shine coming back. Not four subjects. One heart, facing the right way, seeing its rust, wiped daily, and starting to shine.
screen: `THE STATIONS: WHICH WAY TO FACE.` · `THE DISEASES: THE RUST, NAMED.` · `THE MANNERS: THE DAILY CLOTH.` · `THE VIRTUES: THE SHINE RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Let the road pass by slowly, patience, gratitude, sincerity, gentleness, justice, contentment, the manners of the table and the road, and wait for the one trait you'd most like to be true of you a year from now. Name it quietly, once, and picture one small wipe of the cloth toward it. If you pray, you can ask Allah for that trait by its name.
Inward path close. The stations, the diseases, the manners and the virtues, gathered into one picture: a heart that rusts, and can be polished. Today's word.
Your line: polish the heart. What gathers can be wiped. Tomorrow a new block begins: the life cycle.

1318.title: The call in the ear
1318.hook: a newborn's first sounds in this world, and a custom that makes them the call to prayer
1318.howItsDone: In some Muslim families a parent or elder softly recites the adhan in a newborn's right ear soon after birth, and some also recite the iqamah in the left ear; others do not keep the custom.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the inward path closed, with a heart that rusts and can be polished. Today a new block begins: the life cycle. Day seventeen heard the adhan from a minaret; today, in a newborn's ear.
screen: `POLISH THE HEART.` · `A NEW BLOCK: THE LIFE CYCLE.`

segments.voice: A hospital room, minutes after a birth. Monitors beeping. Someone crying, someone laughing, someone already on the phone. And in some Muslim families, a father or grandfather leans down close to the baby's right ear and, very softly, says: Allahu akbar. Allah is greater. Then the rest of the call to prayer, whispered, to someone who has never heard a word. The first words, before the name, before anything else.
screen: `MINUTES AFTER A BIRTH.` → `A WHISPER IN THE RIGHT EAR.` → `ALLAHU AKBAR, FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the source. It isn't a verse of the Qur'an. It's a report from Abu Rafi', who served the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In Sunan Abu Dawud and Jami' at-Tirmidhi, he says, in paraphrase: I saw the Messenger of Allah give the call to prayer in the ear of al-Hasan ibn 'Ali when Fatimah gave birth to him. Al-Hasan was the Prophet's grandson, so the custom traces back to a grandfather leaning over a newborn. Second, the strength of the report. Tirmidhi graded it sound, and noted that people acted on it. Some scholars have questioned its chain. So you'll find families who keep the custom carefully and others who don't, and both have reasons. Some families also say the iqamah, the second call that begins a prayer, in the left ear, following other reports. Third, the words: Allahu akbar; I bear witness there is no god but Allah; I bear witness Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; come to prayer; come to success. Said to a baby, it's not a summons to get up and pray. It's more like a welcome: the first thing this person hears is the name of Allah and the shape of the life ahead. Fourth, a reflection some readers share. They note that the funeral prayer has no call before it, and say a life is lived between the two: the call whispered at birth, and the prayer said at the end. The time in between is how long it takes to answer.
screen: `ABU RAFI': AL-HASAN'S EAR.` · `A REPORT, GRADED AND DEBATED.` · `THE WORDS OF THE ADHAN.` · `A LIFE BETWEEN CALL AND PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Think of a baby born recently, in your family, among friends, or one you only heard about; if no one comes to mind, think of all the babies being born somewhere during this breath. Picture a small face, and the first sounds reaching that ear. If you pray, you can make du'a for that child by name, or for every child born today; if not, hold one wish for them: that the first words they hear be kind ones.
The call in the ear. The adhan whispered into a newborn's right ear, from the report of Abu Rafi' about al-Hasan, so the first words a child hears are Allahu akbar. Today's word.

1319.title: The date
1319.hook: Anas carries a newborn and a handful of dates across Medina
1319.howItsDone: Muslim families who keep the custom perform tahnik soon after birth: a softened date is touched to the inside of the baby's mouth, sometimes by a respected or pious person, with a du'a for blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the call in the ear, the first words a child hears. After the first sound comes the first taste.

Umm Sulaym has just given birth, and her son Anas is carrying the newborn through Medina to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. She has sent some dates along with him. Anas tells the story in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase. The Prophet takes the baby and asks: is there anything with him? Yes, some dates. He takes one, chews it until it's soft, and puts a little of it into the baby's mouth. Today's word is that small act: tahnik.
screen: `ANAS CARRIES A NEWBORN.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING WITH HIM?` → `A SOFTENED DATE FOR THE BABY.`

segments.voice: In Bukhari, the Prophet then named the baby 'Abdullah. Sahih Muslim keeps a fuller telling, in paraphrase: the baby moved his tongue and licked at the date, and the Prophet said, see the Ansar's love of dates. The Ansar were the people of Medina, and dates were their harvest. A joke, a taste and a name, all in one visit. And it happens again. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari tells, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: a son was born to me, and I took him to the Prophet. He named him Ibrahim, did tahnik for him with a date, prayed for blessing for him, and gave him back to me. So it wasn't a single moment in one family; the Prophet did it more than once, when newborns were brought to him. What is it? A date is softened, by chewing or by mashing, and a little is touched to the inside of the baby's mouth, at the palate. In Abu Musa's report it comes with a du'a for blessing. Some Muslim families still keep the custom, and some ask a respected, pious person to do it. Why a date? The texts don't explain it, and it's honest to say so. They only show it: in the moment of welcome, the Prophet reached for something sweet. Before the baby could know a single word, he gave it a taste, and a prayer.
screen: `SEE HOW THE ANSAR LOVE DATES.` · `ABU MUSA: IBRAHIM, A DATE, A DU'A.` · `A SOFTENED DATE TO THE PALATE.` · `THE TEXTS SHOW IT; THEY DON'T EXPLAIN.`

segments.voice: If you have a date or anything sweet nearby, hold it, or picture one, and look at it before you take one slow bite. Let it sit on your tongue the way it would for someone tasting sweetness for the first time. If you pray, you can say bismillah before and alhamdulillah after; if not, simply notice the sweetness, and who might have made it reach you.
Tahnik. Touching a softened date to a newborn's palate, with a prayer for blessing, as the Prophet did for babies brought to him. Today's word.
Your line: sweetness first. A taste and a prayer, before any word. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1320.title: The naming
1320.hook: a name chosen, a name changed, and a man who refused to change his
1320.howItsDone: Muslim parents choose a name with a good meaning for a newborn, on the day of birth or on the seventh day, and names such as 'Abdullah and 'Abd al-Rahman are favored after the hadith in Sahih Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tahnik, sweetness first. In both of yesterday's stories, the date came with a name. Today, the name.

Rough ground. Hard, rugged ground. That's what the name Hazn means, and a man who carried it comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The Prophet asks his name, hears it, and offers him another: Sahl, easy, smooth ground. Hazn says no. I won't change a name my father gave me. His grandson tells this story in Sahih al-Bukhari, and adds a quiet line of his own: that roughness stayed in the family afterward. A name, in this story, is not just a label.
screen: `HAZN: ROUGH GROUND.` → `OFFERED SAHL: EASY GROUND.` → `HE KEEPS HIS FATHER'S NAME.`

segments.voice: Names go back to the beginning. In surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "And He taught Adam all the names." In the Qur'an, the names are what Allah teaches Adam. Then, when. Some reports have the Prophet naming a baby the day it was brought to him: Abu Musa's son Ibrahim, Umm Sulaym's son 'Abdullah, both from yesterday. Another report, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, mentions naming on the seventh day, along with other things done that day that belong to the coming lessons. So families name on the first day, or the seventh, and both have a basis. What makes a name good? In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says, in paraphrase: the most beloved of your names to Allah are 'Abdullah and 'Abd al-Rahman. Servant of Allah. Servant of the Most Merciful. A name that says whose the child is. And names can be changed. Also in Muslim, Ibn 'Umar reports that a daughter of 'Umar was named 'Asiyah, which sounds like disobedient, and the Prophet renamed her Jamilah: beautiful. That's the background to Hazn's story. More than once, the Prophet lifted a heavy name into a lighter one, and Hazn chose to keep his. A name is one of the earliest gifts a child is handed. Every time someone calls them, its meaning gets said out loud.
screen: `HE TAUGHT ADAM ALL THE NAMES.` · `THE FIRST DAY, OR THE SEVENTH.` · `'ABDULLAH, 'ABD AL-RAHMAN.` · `'ASIYAH BECOMES JAMILAH.`

segments.voice: Say your own name silently, slowly, the way someone who loves you says it, and wonder who chose it: for a grandparent, a saint, a sound someone liked, a hope? If your name were a meaning said out loud every time you're called, what would you want it to say? If you pray, you can make du'a for whoever named you.
The naming. A good name given on the first day or the seventh, beloved when it says whose the child is, and changed when the meaning is heavy. Today's word.
Your line: a good name. Hazn kept his; 'Asiyah became Jamilah. Tomorrow, the seventh-day sacrifice.

1321.title: The seventh-day sacrifice
1321.hook: a week-old baby, a sheep, and a meal shared in thanks
1321.howItsDone: Muslim families who hold the 'aqiqah slaughter a sheep or goat for a newborn, traditionally on the seventh day, and share the meat with relatives, neighbors and people in need, following their own scholars on how strongly it is urged.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the naming, on the first day or the seventh, beloved when it says whose the child is. That seventh-day report named other things done that day. Here is one.

Seven days after a birth, the backyard fills up. Pots the size of laundry baskets. Rice, meat, aunties arguing happily about salt. Neighbors who've never met the baby carrying plates home. Somewhere in the middle of it, a tired mother and father, and a week-old child sleeping through the whole thing. The meat on those plates comes from a sheep slaughtered in thanks for this one small person. That slaughter has a name: the 'aqiqah.
screen: `A BACKYARD, A WEEK AFTER BIRTH.` → `PLATES GOING HOME.` → `A SHEEP, IN THANKS.`

segments.voice: First, the words. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Salman ibn 'Amir reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase: with the boy there is an 'aqiqah, so shed blood on his behalf, and remove harm from him. That second half belongs to tomorrow. Today, the first: blood shed for a child, as an act of thanks. Second, the day. Samurah reports, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, in paraphrase: every boy is held in pledge by his 'aqiqah, which is slaughtered for him on the seventh day. Held in pledge is a striking phrase, and its meaning is discussed. Some readers hear it as a debt of thanks that belongs to the child's arrival. Third, girls and boys. Umm Kurz reports, in Abu Dawud, in paraphrase: for a boy, two sheep that are alike, and for a girl, one. So the 'aqiqah is for daughters as well as sons. How strongly it's urged, and the details of day and number, are questions families take to their own scholars, and they follow their means. Fourth, the meal. Tradition says the 'aqiqah isn't eaten alone: it's cooked, shared with relatives and neighbors, and part is given to people in need. A week after a birth, when a new family could easily close the door and sleep, the custom opens the door and sets out plates. A child's arrival becomes good news for the street. Thanks, in the 'aqiqah, isn't only said. It's served.
screen: `WITH THE BOY, AN 'AQIQAH.` · `HELD IN PLEDGE, THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `FOR DAUGHTERS AND FOR SONS.` · `THANKS SERVED ON PLATES.`

segments.voice: Think of a child whose birth you're glad of, a new baby you know, a niece or nephew, your own child, or, if it fits, the day you were born and whoever was glad of you. Hold that gladness a moment, and picture one small share of food in that child's name, a plate taken next door or a box of sweets brought to work. If you pray, you can thank Allah for that child by name.
'Aqiqah. The sacrifice for a newborn, on the seventh day in Samurah's report, for daughters and sons, its meat shared with family, neighbors and those in need. Today's word.
Your line: thanks for a child. Said out loud, and then served on plates. See you tomorrow.

1322.title: Shaving the hair
1322.hook: a baby's first hair, weighed, and its weight in silver given away
1322.howItsDone: On or around the seventh day, some Muslim families shave the newborn's head and give the weight of the hair in silver, or its value in money, to charity, alongside the 'aqiqah and the naming.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the 'aqiqah, a sacrifice on the seventh day, and your line, thanks for a child. That same seventh day holds one more custom, and it fits in the palm of a hand.

A grandson has been born. His name is al-Hasan, and his mother is Fatimah, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The baby can't hold anything, can't say anything, can't do a single thing for anyone. And the Prophet gives his daughter an instruction about the softest, lightest thing the baby has: the hair he was born with. Not to keep it. Not to throw it away. To weigh it.

segments.voice: Here's the report, in Jami' at-Tirmidhi, in paraphrase. When al-Hasan was born, the Prophet said to Fatimah: shave his head, and give the weight of his hair in silver as charity. So they weighed it, the report says, and it came to a dirham, or part of a dirham. A coin, maybe less. The amount is small, and the hadith says so plainly. The point isn't the size of the gift. Something taken from the child becomes something given in the child's name. Second, the half-sentence left over from yesterday. The hadith in Bukhari said: shed blood on the child's behalf, and remove harm from him. What harm? The hadith doesn't say, and some readers take it to mean this very thing: the hair the baby was born with. And a hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, in paraphrase, sets the seventh day in one line: the 'aqiqah sacrificed, the head shaved, the child named. Third, what families do now. Some still shave the baby's head on the seventh day and weigh the hair. Others estimate the weight and give its value in money. Scholars discuss the details, and families follow the school and the custom they know. Fourth, look at it from the baby's side. A baby owns nothing, can't earn, can't even hold a coin. And yet, on day seven, there's already charity written in the baby's name. Before a child can do a single good deed, the family does one for them. The child arrives in the world as a giver.
screen: `SHAVE IT. WEIGH IT. GIVE ITS WEIGHT.` · `A DIRHAM, OR PART OF ONE.` · `SACRIFICE, SHAVING, NAMING.` · `A BABY ARRIVES AS A GIVER.`

segments.voice: Bring one child to mind: your own, a niece, a neighbor's new baby, or the child you once were, and say their name quietly. Think of something small that could be given in that name, a coin in a box or a meal for someone; the hadith's amount wasn't large either. If you pray, ask good for that child in your own words; if not, just hold their name and the gift together.
Shaving the hair. On the seventh day, a baby's first hair is shaved, and its weight in silver is given away in charity. Today's word.
Your line: weight in silver. Something light, given in a name that can't give yet. Until tomorrow.

1323.title: Circumcision, the way of Ibrahim
1323.hook: five habits of the fitrah, and the one traced to Ibrahim
1323.howItsDone: Muslim families circumcise boys as part of the fitrah and the way of Ibrahim; the timing varies by family and culture, from the first days of life to later childhood, sometimes with a family celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the baby's first hair, shaved and weighed, and your line, weight in silver. Today, one more custom of early life.

Five small habits, listed in one sentence. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says five things belong to the fitrah, the natural way people are made. In paraphrase: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, trimming the mustache, clipping the nails, and plucking the armpit hair. Four of them are done again and again. The first one is different. It's done once, and tradition traces it back to a single person: Ibrahim.
screen: `FIVE THINGS OF THE FITRAH.` → `FOUR, DONE AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `ONE, DONE ONCE.`

segments.voice: Khitan means circumcision: for a boy, the removal of the foreskin. The Qur'an doesn't spell it out; the teaching comes through hadith, and through one name. In another report in Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet says that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, circumcised himself with an adze, and the report says he was eighty years old. An old man, keeping a sign in his own body. Why does Ibrahim carry so much weight here? The Qur'an tells the Prophet to follow him. In Pickthall's translation: "Follow the religion of Abraham, as one by nature upright." Upright by nature: close to the idea of fitrah. So Muslims keep khitan as part of the millah of Ibrahim, the way of Ibrahim, carried on by those who follow him. Then a neighbor. Jews trace circumcision to Abraham too, in the book of Genesis, as a sign of the covenant. Two families of faith, one shared ancestor, and a shared mark. Then the schools. Muslim scholars differ on how binding it is: some schools count it obligatory, others a strongly emphasized sunnah. And families choose different times: some on the seventh day, some later in childhood, some with a celebration. Last, respect. This is a custom of the body and of the family. The way to learn about it is the way anyone would want their own customs learned: listen, ask kindly, and let the people who keep it explain what it means to them.
screen: `KHITAN, TRACED TO IBRAHIM.` · `FOLLOW THE RELIGION OF ABRAHAM.` · `A MARK SHARED WITH A NEIGHBOR.` · `THE SCHOOLS WEIGH IT DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Think of a custom from your own family that marks a child as belonging: a name, a blessing, a first haircut, a photo on the wall. Picture someone asking about it kindly and really listening, and notice how that feels. Then think of one kind question you could ask about a custom that isn't yours, and how you'd listen to the answer.
